description: AP SpaceLabs is a team of young innovators powered by AP Education, passionate about STEM, technology, and space exploration. We turn curiosity into creativity and ideas into innovative solutions to real-world challenges. Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to collaborate, learn, and create a positive impact on Earth and beyond.
summary:
ORBITA-7: 72 Hours to Survive on Mars is a turn-based web simulation that trains young players to think like mission operators. The player manages Base Alpha-7, a fictional Martian colony hit by a planet-wide dust storm, across six 12-hour turns. Each turn presents an emergency, such as dusty solar panels, an ice extractor failure, a radiation alert, an oxygen system fault, a habitat leak, and the preparation of a supply ship's arrival. Players choose between three options, and every choice affects four indicators: energy, life support, water and supplies, and crew safety.

Short pixel-art cutscenes show the cause and the result of each decision, so players see why a system fails or recovers. No option is always best, which teaches trade-offs and how a base's systems depend on each other. The game is inspired by NASA information on Martian dust storms, radiation, subsurface ice, and the MOXIE oxygen experiment. It is available in English and Spanish, making space science and mission thinking accessible and engaging for the next generation of explorers.
details:
ORBITA-7 is a turn-based web game set in 2042 at Base Alpha-7, a fictional Martian colony. A planet-wide dust storm cuts solar power and communications, and a supply ship waits in orbit. Over six 12-hour turns (72 hours), the player acts as Operations Director. Each turn shows an emergency and three options. Every choice changes four indicators (energy, life support, water and supplies, crew safety) and mission flags (communications, landing zone, base repair). After each turn, the base consumes resources, and the player sees a short lesson explaining why the decision helped or hurt.

Before choosing, a short cutscene shows the cause of the problem. After choosing, another cutscene shows the action: a rover cleaning panels, astronauts leaving the airlock, or equipment shutting down. The base scene also changes with the indicators: lights dim when energy is low, crops wither when water is scarce, and the signal to the supply ship connects or breaks. The final screen shows one of four endings, a timeline of decisions, and key learnings.

ORBITA-7 helps young people understand that a space base is a system of connected resources, where saving energy, protecting the crew and repairing equipment compete. There is no always-best option, so players learn trade-offs and critical thinking. It is playable in a browser, needs no installation, and is available in English and Spanish.

Instead of showing numbers only, the game turns each consequence into something visible. It combines pixel-art cutscenes, a base that changes with the player's choices, and very little text, so the learning happens through seeing and deciding.

We considered scientific honesty: the indicators are educational abstractions, not real measurements, and we separate real technology (the MOXIE experiment) from fictional colony systems. We tested different decision paths so that several endings are possible and no option dominates. We designed for ages 12 to 14, using short text, large icons, and clear feedback.

We built the web app with React, JavaScript, CSS and Vite, with pixel-art assets and cutscenes, and used Git and GitHub for version control. We used Antigravity, an AI coding assistant, to help build and refine the code and interface.
